metadata.note: Yes -- Pierre, South Dakota (the state capital) had rail service two decades before 1900. The Chicago and North Western Railroad's 'Dakota Central' division built west from Tracy, Minnesota through Volga, De Smet (the town Laura Ingalls Wilder's family homesteaded near, made famous in her Little House books -- her father worked for this railroad), and Huron (used as construction headquarters) to Pierre, completing the line in 1880. Geometry is real-traced from OpenStreetMap active-rail geometry for the Tracy-Volga-De Smet-Huron stretch. The final Huron-Pierre stretch (~170km) could NOT be matched to any connected rail path, active or abandoned, in OSM's data for this area -- only a handful of small, disconnected abandoned-rail fragments exist near each end, not enough to stitch a real trace -- so that segment is an honest straight-line approximation, flagged rather than guessed at false precision. It's plausible this specific stretch has been so thoroughly removed (rail lifted, grade plowed under for farmland, a common fate for prairie branch lines) that no trace remains in OpenStreetMap at all.
sources: https://historicpierrefortpierre.com/chicago-and-north-western-railroad-bridge/ (C&NW laid track to Pierre by 1880; expanded west across the Missouri River to Rapid City starting 1905-07 via subsidiary Pierre, Rapid City and North Western)

properties.line: Chicago and North Western: Winona – Rapid City
properties.speed_source: estimated: 1880s prairie branch-line steam rail; unsourced

segments.note: The Winona and St. Peter Railroad (part of C&NW from 1867) built west from Winona, MN through Mankato, reaching Tracy by the early 1870s; the Dakota Central division continued it to Pierre, SD by 1880. The Missouri River had no permanent crossing at Pierre until the Chicago and North Western Railroad Bridge, built 1906-07 (first train Oct 14, 1907), finally linking this line through to Rapid City via the Pierre, Rapid City and Northwestern Railroad on the west bank - completing one continuous route from the Mississippi River to the Black Hills. Frequency estimated across the full span, unsourced. PASSENGER SERVICE CONFIRMED TO 1951 by the Feb 1952 Official Guide (C&NW Tables 60 and 67). 1951 IS THE LAST CONFIRMED YEAR, NOT A KNOWN END — no source consulted dates when passengers actually stopped, and service certainly continued after it; the Dakota 400 west of Huron is usually put in the early 1960s, and C&NW's absolute last intercity day was 30 April 1971. Do not extend without evidence. This segment previously ended at 1995, which is the Union Pacific merger — a corporate date, not a passenger one, and 44 years of overstated service.
sources: Segment-level: end year confirmed to 1951 from the source below; start year 1907 is the documented completion of the Pierre bridge. The end is an open floor, not an ending.
Official Guide of the Railways, Feb 1952 edition (schedules effective 30 Sept 1951), Chicago and North Western System section — local copy research/sources/official_guide_1952.txt
